title: The Jewish Model of Atonement
hook: Did Israel's sacrifices calm an angry God, or clean his house?
tldr: Israel never sacrificed to soothe God's wrath or restore his honor; that was pagan thinking. Sacrifices meant thanks, communion, cleansing and covenant renewal. The sin offering's blood purified God's dwelling like a disinfectant, and the guilt offering was compensation. Jesus' blood likewise cleanses and covers, with no torment involved.
big_idea: Atonement cleanses and covers sin; it never punishes or tortures.

points.title: Sacrifice was not appeasement
points.text: Pagans killed to avoid punishment from capricious gods. Israel's sacrifices were thanksgiving, communion, worship, cleansing, purification and covenant renewal: realigning with God's will.

points.title: A hospital picture
points.text: Israel was the hospital, the Tabernacle the operating room, the altar the operating table, the priests the surgeons. Impurity had to be kept out of God's holy, unique dwelling.

points.title: Hata'at: the purification offering
points.text: Its blood was sprinkled on the tent and instruments like a sanitizer. Jesus' blood likewise washes robes white: it cleanses, it does not vent wrath.

points.title: Asham: the guilt offering
points.text: An individual's compensation for an offense, like paying a parking fine, treating sin as stealing from God. No abuse, wrath or violence was part of it.

points.title: Blood means life
points.text: Life is in the blood. In ancient Judaism blood symbolized healing, purification and life, not violence. Donating blood is giving life.

points.title: Kaphar: wipe away and cover
points.text: Atonement may mean erasing sin or covering it. Perhaps both: Old Testament sacrifices covered sin, and the Lamb of God takes it away.

sections.summary: Israel never sacrificed to relax God's wrath or satisfy an appetite for blood, as Calvin's and Anselm's theories suggest. Sacrifices were not corpses offered so God would be satisfied and spare Israel (PSA), nor about restoring God's lost honor (Satisfaction Atonement). Those were pagan motives. For Israel, sacrifice meant thanks, communion, worship, cleansing, purification and covenant renewal: repentance and devotion. The Torah lists many sacrifices, but only two dealt directly with forgiveness: Asham (guilt) and Hata'at (sin or purification).

sections.h: The Book of Atonement in a Nutshell
sections.summary: Leviticus mentions atonement about fifty times, often with blood, and opens with God calling sinful Israel's leader to fellowship (Leviticus 1:1). The Day of Atonement is its heart. God helps Israel live in his presence through rituals, seven annual feasts and mediating priests. Eight chapters guard purity: reproductive fluids, skin disease, mold or a dead body defiled the Tabernacle. Such impurities of death have no hold on God but were banned from his dwelling.

sections.h: The hospital and the operating room
sections.summary: Picture Israel as a hospital, the Tabernacle as the operating room, the altar as the operating table and the priests as surgeons. The closer to the altar, the more serious a breach of purity. Holy means unique or different, so God's dwelling is sacred; bringing impurity in would make it no longer distinct. Sacrifices fall into four to eight categories and 20-30 subtypes, but those dealing with sin were the minority.

Three Hebrew words, often all translated the same in English, underlie atonement: Gaal (redeem, kinsman), Padah (liberate, redeem) and Kaphar (atone, forgive). They mostly describe redeeming: settling a family debt, a relative reclaiming property, freeing an animal or slave by covering its cost, or paying a substitute for a life. Corporal punishment or torment was never part of Israel's sacrificial system.

Kaphar appears over a hundred times and gives Yom Kippur its name. Some scholars read it as void, wipe away, remove: sin erased and the sinner restored to innocence (Isaiah 44:22, Zechariah 3:4). Others read cover or hide: sin remains but is concealed, sparing the sinner its repercussions (Psalm 32:1, Psalm 85:3). Perhaps both: Old Testament sacrifices covered sin, and Jesus' sacrifice removed it. John's Lamb who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29) sees atonement as collective.

Hata'at comes from a root shared by Het (sin) and Hite (disinfect, cleanse, purify), so translations say sin offering or purification offering. Scholars mostly favor purification. Its blood was sprinkled in the tent and on instruments like sanitizer in an operating room. The point was not the animal's death as punishment, but blood (life, Leviticus 17:11) cleansing sin (death and sickness). Jesus' blood washing robes white (Revelation 7:14, Hebrews 10:10) only makes sense as Hata'at: it cleanses and purifies us.

Asham means guilt. It was compensation for an offense, made only by an individual for their own transgression, unlike communal offerings. Rabbi Yonatan Grossman notes its law focuses on the financial aspect: an animal of set monetary worth. Sin has a price, like a fine for parking in a no-parking zone. It treated sin as stealing from God, a breach of trust needing compensation. No abuse, wrath or violence was involved.

Hollywood links blood with violence; the Torah says life is in the blood (Leviticus 17:11), as science agrees. Donating blood gives life, which is why drinking Jesus' blood brings eternal life (John 6:54). Sacrificial blood was like alcohol gel, bleach or detergent: no surgeon enters an unsanitized room. Ignoring sacrifices was like telling God he was not wanted, so his presence no longer shielded Israel from enemies (God's wrath). Sacrifice fostered fellowship, blessing and protection, unlike pagan appeasement of sadistic gods.

sections.h: Tim Mackie: a pagan story imported
sections.summary: Tim Mackie, founder of The Bible Project, says many inherited a pagan story: angry gods appeased by an animal's death. Popular Christianity imported it into Leviticus and the cross: a holy God hates you and must kill you, but kills an animal or Jesus instead, so Jesus rescues us from God. The tragic irony is that an expression of God's love is twisted into something dark. With enough biblical language to pass, the story is an imposter once Leviticus and the New Testament speak for themselves.

sections.h: Michael Heiser: resurrection, not violent death
sections.summary: Old Testament scholar Michael S. Heiser (1963-2023) asked whether God intended Jesus' death as penal substitution or foreknew it and endorsed him by raising him. God foreknew humanity would lose immortality, and death separated him from those he loved. Death was everyone's problem, so the focal point is resurrection. Redeem means buy back. We are guilty for our own sins (his view of Romans 5:12). Christ was not God venting anger on his Son but defeating death, though a sufficient death was still needed.

The PSA view that Mackie and Heiser criticize entered Western Christianity through brilliant but flawed figures: Augustine, Anselm, Calvin, Luther and Edwards, who shaped conservative doctrines of atonement and hellfire. Their strong antisemitic attitudes pushed them away from the Jewish context and the Old Testament writings.

Torment, torture and abuse tied to PSA and Hellfire were alien to Israel's atonement. From a Jewish view, Jesus' atonement cleanses the stain of sin and restores purity: his blood purifies us from all sin (1 John 1:7), echoing atonement as erasure. It is also a covering that protects: Paul calls Jesus a sacrifice of atonement, hilasterion, a covering or expiation (Romans 3:25). Cleansing and covering both find full expression in Jesus' life, death and resurrection, reconciling humanity to God.

mythfact.myth: Israel's sacrifices were meant to appease God's wrath.
mythfact.fact: Appeasement was the pagan motive. Israel's sacrifices meant thanksgiving, communion, cleansing, purification and covenant renewal.

mythfact.myth: In sacrifice, the animal's death was the punishment that mattered.
mythfact.fact: In the Hata'at the point was its blood, representing life, used to purify the sanctuary and instruments.

mythfact.myth: Blood in the Bible is about violence.
mythfact.fact: Life is in the blood. In ancient Judaism blood symbolized healing, purification and life, not wrath.

mythfact.myth: On the cross, Jesus rescues us from God.
mythfact.fact: Tim Mackie calls this a pagan imposter story; Heiser sees God defeating death through resurrection, not venting anger on his Son.

quotes.text: Much of popular Christian belief has simply imported a pagan storyline into Leviticus and the stories about Jesus’ death on the cross.
Christ wasn’t God's chance to vent his anger on his Son. It was his chance to defeat death with resurrection
In the context of ancient Judaism, blood symbolizes not wrath but healing, purification, and life.

quiz.q: What did the Hata'at's blood do?
quiz.why: Like sanitizer in an operating room, it purified the tent, altar and instruments of sin's defilement.

quiz.q: What was the Asham, the guilt offering?
options: Compensation by an individual for an offense
quiz.why: It was an individual's payment of set monetary worth, like a parking fine, with no wrath or violence.

quiz.q: According to Heiser, what is the focal point of God's plan?
quiz.why: Death was humanity's problem; God defeated it through resurrection rather than venting anger on his Son.

reflect: If sacrifice was about welcoming God's presence, what in your life keeps him out of the room?
